summary:
**TerraTwin: Earth Analog Discovery Platform**

TerraTwin is an interactive planetary-analog research atlas developed by Team AstroAnalytica for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Its objective is to identify and characterize Earth environments that share specific geological and environmental characteristics with the Moon and Mars.

Our project investigates four Indian locations: Lonar Crater, Deccan Traps, Spiti Valley and the Rann of Kutch. Each location offers unique research opportunities involving impact geology, volcanism, cold-desert processes and saline environments.

Through an interactive map, location profiles and planetary comparison features, TerraTwin aims to help users explore these environments, understand their scientific relevance and examine supporting evidence.

The platform follows four main stages: Discover, Describe, Compare and Verify. It also emphasizes reliable data sources, scientific transparency and research limitations.

Our vision is to connect Earth's geological diversity with planetary exploration and make analog research easier to explore, understand and evaluate.

TERRATWIN

Earth locations that help us investigate the Moon and Mars

NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

Team AstroAnalytica

Explore • Compare • Verify

An interactive research atlas for discovering and characterizing terrestrial environments that share specific geological and environmental characteristics with the Moon and Mars.

1. Project overview — What exactly is TerraTwin?

TerraTwin is a proposed web-based research platform that helps users discover and investigate locations on Earth that can serve as analog environments for studying the Moon and Mars.

The word analog means something that shares particular characteristics with something else.

For example:

  • A crater on Earth can help researchers investigate impact-related geological processes that also occur on the Moon and Mars.
  • Volcanic rock formations on Earth can help researchers study volcanic processes found on other planetary bodies.
  • Cold deserts and saline environments can help researchers investigate certain environmental and geological processes relevant to planetary exploration.

However, Earth, the Moon and Mars are not identical. They have different atmospheres, gravity, surface conditions and geological histories.

Therefore, TerraTwin focuses on comparing specific scientific characteristics and processes rather than claiming that two environments are identical.


2. The actual problem we are solving

Imagine that scientists are preparing equipment and scientific instruments for a future lunar or Martian mission.

Before taking that equipment into space, researchers need to understand how it performs in challenging environments. They may need to test:

  • Geological mapping techniques.
  • Surface imaging methods.
  • Rock and soil investigation procedures.
  • Instrument operation.
  • Field research workflows.

Earth provides accessible environments for studying selected geological processes and testing methods.

But there is a problem: not every potentially useful terrestrial analog site has been properly characterized.

This is where TerraTwin comes in.

Our project aims to organize candidate locations, describe their geological and environmental features, compare those features with planetary processes and show what additional evidence is required.

Our central research question is:

"How can we identify and characterize Earth's geological and environmental locations that can help us understand the Moon and Mars?"

3. Our four selected Earth locations

This is one of the most important parts of your project. We have selected four Indian environments, each representing a different geological or environmental characteristic.

Location 1 — Lonar Crater, Maharashtra

Impact geology

Lonar Crater is an impact structure formed in Deccan basalt. It is particularly interesting because it allows researchers to investigate the geological effects of an impact event.

What we want to study:

  • Crater shape and morphology.
  • Impact-related geological materials.
  • Rocks and minerals affected by impact processes.
  • Methods for mapping and examining crater structures.

Connection with the Moon and Mars:

Both the Moon and Mars have impact craters. Studying an impact structure on Earth can help researchers investigate selected aspects of crater formation and impact-modified materials.

Our research question: Which geological features of Lonar Crater can be compared with impact structures on the Moon and Mars?

Location 2 — Deccan Traps, Western India

Volcanic geology

The Deccan Traps are a large volcanic basalt province. They provide an opportunity to investigate volcanic rocks and lava-flow landforms.

What we want to study:

  • Basaltic rock formations.
  • Volcanic landforms.
  • Lava-flow structures.
  • Surface characteristics of volcanic terrain.

Connection with the Moon and Mars:

The Moon has extensive basaltic volcanic plains, and Mars also has a history of volcanism. Comparing volcanic formations on Earth with planetary volcanic features can help researchers understand these geological processes.

Our research question: How do the basaltic formations of the Deccan Traps compare with selected lunar and Martian volcanic terrains?

panoramic view of spiti valley, india

Location 3 — Spiti Valley, Himachal Pradesh

Cold-desert environment

Spiti Valley is a high-altitude cold-desert environment. Its barren terrain and temperature variations make it an interesting candidate for studying weathering and freeze–thaw processes.

What we want to study:

  • Temperature variation.
  • High-altitude environmental conditions.
  • Weathering processes.
  • Freeze–thaw effects on rocks and terrain.

Connection with Mars:

Mars is a cold, dusty world with evidence of ancient water and geological processes. Spiti can provide a terrestrial environment for studying selected cold-desert processes.

Our research question: How do temperature variations and weathering processes in Spiti Valley compare with selected Martian surface processes?

Location 4 — Rann of Kutch, Gujarat

Saline and evaporitic environments

The Rann of Kutch is known for its saline environment and evaporitic features.

What we want to study:

  • Salt deposits.
  • Evaporation-related geological processes.
  • Saline surface characteristics.
  • Arid-environment processes.

Connection with Mars:

Mars has geological evidence of salts and minerals associated with ancient water-related processes. Studying terrestrial saline and evaporitic environments can help researchers investigate some of these processes.

Our research question: What can the saline and evaporitic environments of the Rann of Kutch teach us about salt-related planetary geology?

These four locations and their intended research comparisons are explicitly described in your presentation. They are candidate analog environments, not confirmed scientific discoveries.

4. Why Lonar Crater is our main case study

Although all four locations are important, your presentation gives special attention to Lonar Crater.

This is a good decision because it gives us a specific example to explain the project's scientific approach.

Against Cloudy Sky Lonar Lake National Monument crater full rim view

Lonar Meteorite Impact Crater - Impactite

5

Let's understand the reasoning.

Step 1: Identify the geological feature.

Lonar is an impact crater formed in basaltic rock.

Step 2: Identify the planetary connection.

The Moon and Mars contain impact craters, so Lonar offers an opportunity to study selected impact-related structures and materials on Earth.

Step 3: Identify measurable characteristics.

We could investigate:

  • Crater diameter and shape.
  • Rim structure.
  • Elevation differences.
  • Slope variations.
  • Exposed rock types.
  • Impact-related geological materials.

Step 4: Compare the evidence.

We would compare the Earth measurements with measurements from selected lunar or Martian craters.

Step 5: Explain the limitations.

Lonar is not a replica of a lunar crater. The comparison is specifically about impact geology, not identical environmental conditions.

This is an important distinction. If a judge asks why Lonar is useful, you should say:

"Lonar Crater is useful because it allows us to investigate impact-related geological structures and materials in an accessible terrestrial environment. We are studying the geological process, not claiming that the crater reproduces the Moon's complete surface environment."


5. How TerraTwin compares Earth, Moon and Mars

This is the scientific heart of the project.

We have three different categories of information:

The important thing is that we are matching geological processes, not just looking at photographs and deciding that two landscapes look similar.

For example, two locations may both look rocky, but that does not prove they have the same rock composition or geological history.

Your comparison should be supported by:

  • Rock types and mineralogy.
  • Crater or lava-flow morphology.
  • Sedimentary and impact features.
  • Temperature range.
  • Elevation and pressure context.
  • Water, ice, salts and aridity.

    6. How the actual TerraTwin website will work

Your project is designed as an interactive research atlas.

Think of it as a digital platform where someone can select an Earth location, investigate its characteristics and compare them with selected planetary processes.

Here is the proposed user journey.

TerraTwin — User workflow

  1. DISCOVER
    The user opens the interactive map and chooses a location, such as Lonar Crater.
    GGWPI | Groundwater, Geophysical and Geospatial Survey Services in India
    ggwp-i.com
  2. DESCRIBE
    The platform displays information about the selected location, including its geology, landforms and environmental characteristics.
    TerraCroma | Platform Capabilities
    terracroma.ai
  3. COMPARE
    The user chooses a relevant lunar or Martian reference region and examines the specific characteristics that can be compared.
    NASA Space Apps Challenge
    spaceappschallenge.org
  4. VERIFY
    The user checks the supporting sources, understands the uncertainty and identifies which additional measurements are needed.
    Full article: Approaches and tools for user-driven provenance and data quality information in spatial data infrastructures
    tandfonline.com

The workflow is deliberately simple:

Discover → Describe → Compare → Verify

The objective is to make each comparison traceable and open to scientific improvement.

7. The similarity scoring system

Your presentation includes an important feature called the Moon and Mars similarity indices.

These scores help users navigate and explore candidate locations.

However, there is something you absolutely must understand before presenting this feature.

Current prototype limitation

The scores shown in the presentation are illustrative.

They are team-assigned qualitative values, not actual measured results and not official NASA ratings.

They must not be presented as scientifically validated results.

How can we make the scoring scientific?

We need to follow a proper process:

  1. Define measurable comparison criteria.
  2. Assign scientifically justified weights.
  3. Collect reliable Earth and planetary measurements.
  4. Normalize the measurements to comparable scales.
  5. Calculate the similarity score.
  6. Report uncertainty and missing data.
  7. Validate the method against published analog research.

A proposed future formula is:

\[ \text{Analog Score}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_i s_i \]

Where:

  • \(w_i\) represents the importance assigned to a feature.
  • \(s_i\) represents its normalized similarity.
  • The sum of all weights should equal 1.

For example, a Lonar Crater comparison could consider crater morphology, elevation, slope and geological evidence.

The score would tell users how similar the selected features are according to the chosen method. It would not tell them whether a location is suitable for a real Moon landing.

This transparency is one of the strongest aspects of your presentation

A scientific comparison needs more than attractive photographs.

Our platform should organize evidence into three categories.

The presentation also identifies useful starting sources:

  • NASA Earth Observatory

  • IUGS Geoheritage

One thing to improve before submission: your presentation currently lists broad organization homepages as starting points. The final research should include exact scientific papers, datasets and image credits that support each specific claim.

9. Why is TerraTwin useful for future space exploration?

This is where we explain the real-world value of our project.

TerraTwin has two major potential applications.

A. Instrument and method testing

Researchers can investigate suitable terrestrial environments for practising:

  • Geological mapping.
  • Rock and soil sampling workflows.
  • Surface imaging.
  • Scientific instrument operations.
  • Field research procedures.

For example, Lonar Crater could be investigated for practising impact-geology mapping methods.

B. Scientific preparation

Terrestrial field studies can help researchers:

  • Understand geological environments.
  • Develop scientific hypotheses.
  • Improve field investigation methods.
  • Anticipate research challenges.
  • Prepare for interpreting observations from other worlds.

Our platform helps identify possible research environments. It does not claim that NASA has selected or already used our four locations.

10. Limitations and future development

A good scientific project must acknowledge what it cannot do.

Our current project has four major limitations:

  1. It has a shortlist of candidate locations rather than an exhaustive global database.
  2. Its qualitative comparisons require stronger scientific measurements.
  3. Its similarity scores are illustrative and not validated.
  4. Environmental and geological conditions can vary across different parts of a location and over time.
